items.desc: Hi. I made small project called Zpup. It takes small 3D scene written in JSON and gives back a flat SVG from any angle. There is no JavaScript in the file, so it works in img-tag or README. I needed 3D for small project at my company, and Zdog make big impression on me. But Zdog has not had a releas
items.author: select1dev
items.descZh: 本项目源于作者在公司小型项目中对轻量级3D技术的需求，受Zdog项目的启发，作者开发了名为Zpup的微型工具。其核心功能是将使用JSON描述的微型3D场景转换为任意角度输出的扁平SVG矢量图。最大的技术亮点在于生成的文件完全不含任何JavaScript代码，确保了极高的安全性与兼容性，可直接嵌入HTML的img标签或Markdown的README文档中。该项目非常适合需要无脚本依赖、跨平台渲染的轻量级3D矢量图形展示场景，如技术文档插图、静态网页图标及开源项目说明。通过JSON输入和纯SVG输出，Zpup为静态3D可视化提供了一种极简且高效的解决方案。
items.quote: 它接收用 JSON 编写的小型 3D 场景，并从任何角度返回一个扁平的 SVG。

items.title: Show HN: Satelital – How I made a custom game engine for my indie game
items.desc: description: Seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch. And Last week I released Satelital, a rulediscovery game about learning alien logic. title: How I made a custom game engine for Satelital image: https://spectralorbit.com/assets/screenshots/trium_2.jpg [](/assets/screenshots/trium%5F2.png) Seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch. And Last week I released Satelital, a rulediscovery game about learning alien logic. As a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch. My motivation was to learn the actual fundamentals behind the technology of videogames. This meant I had to build most of the tools I would need myself, including the game engine, renderer, puzzles, editors, UX, design, art and music. Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it. The main reason I got into programming was the idea of eventually working on games. I spent many years working on web and building mobile apps. It was fun, but I felt like I wasn't going in the direction I really wanted to. So one day, after listening to every Jonathan Blow talk I could find and playing too much The Witness, I decided to finally give it a try. I spent many days and countless hours looking for the best tool I could use to make a game, but nothing left me satisfied. The closest I got to having fun with gamedev was with the [LÖVE framework](https://love2d.org/) making a few jam games. But even with that, it felt quite limiting to not really know what was happening behind the graphics I somehow managed to animate on my screen. [](/blog/assets/love%5F2d%5Fgrid.jpg) Early prototype of a tilebased level editor built with LÖVE and Lua. I remember hearing about shaders and parallel programming. The concept always felt very arcane and mysterious to me, but now writing them is the thing I enjoy the most while coding. I finally decided to jump into the swimming pool and actually learn C⁠+⁠+. I had to learn how to manage memory and how not to shoot myself in the foot with the wrong tools. I started using SDL2 while trying to use the C⁠+⁠+ standard library as little as possible. Before getting too deep into the engine, I actually finished a prototype of the puzzles not long after learning how to draw some simple graphics with C⁠+⁠+. It had very early versions of four kinds of puzzles that mostly survived until the final game. It was made entirely with SDL2, but I soon realised that if I wanted more interesting graphics, I would need to use shaders and decided to switch to OpenGL. Early prototype gameplay with SDL2 This puzzle was the first one I made, also the only one that survived until the end With the help of [LearnOpenGL](https://learnopengl.com/) I quickly had a triangle on the screen. From there, learning things like lighting, tonemapping, normal maps, shader effects and everything else opened up a whole new way of looking at computers for me. Before, my idea of how a computer actually draws to the screen was quite naive. When I started learning graphics I just wanted to be able to manually change the color of each pixel individually, but in the end the idea of running a program in parallel for every pixel clicked for me. One thing that made a huge difference while working on shaders was having code reloading. Before that, I had a complex system that stored constant values in config files, which would later get passed through uniforms into shaders. Then a custom development menu would provide some UI to tweak those values at runtime. With that I stopped having to reload and compile everything for every little change I wanted to make. It worked, but having to maintain all this extra scaffolding was slowing me down. Another unexpected downside of this setup was that, in some cases, the shader compiler couldn't optimize the code as well as it otherwise could, since knowing constant values ahead of time helps it make better decisions. Having shader reloading made a huge difference. Being able to change some code, save the file and immediately see the result on screen was very useful. Iterating on shaders became much faster and more fun. This was probably my biggest regret about not having it from day one. Color modification preview using shader hot reloading For a big part of the development I was using SDL2, mainly to create a window, read input and get a surface to draw on. But it felt wrong to depend on a library that was several times bigger than my entire game just to handle a few seemingly simple tasks. I decided to drop that dependency and make my own platform layer that I could understand and maintain. I wouldn't have to wait for someone else to fix a bug anymore because now I could just change it myself. It wasn't that hard to end up with a single file with a few thousand lines of code that supported both macOS and Windows. I'm now looking forward to working on mobile and console ports, it feels like it might be a fun thing to work on. At some point during development, compile times were getting longer, so I decided to look into what was going on. I checked where all that time was going, and to my surprise a lot of it was spent compiling standard library things. Stuff like std::function was particularly slow for example. Eventually I realised that I wasn't actually forced to use the standard library just because it was there, and the subset I needed wasn't that hard to implement myself. It took me a month to replace it with my own base library, but it was so worth it. Not only did compile times get faster, but I also learned how a lot of things I had always taken for granted in other languages actually worked. At some point I started looking into Vulkan because I wanted HDR. I couldn't get it working on macOS through OpenGL and I was worried about OpenGL being deprecated in the future. Also I didn't really want to build the whole engine around an API that might become deprecated. [](/blog/asse
items.author: ellipticaldoor
items.descZh: 一位拥有多年Web与移动应用开发经验的开发者，因受到《The Witness》等作品启发，决定用七年时间从零开始打造一款名为Satelital的规则发现类游戏，其核心动机是深入掌握电子游戏技术的根本原理。为实现这一目标，他未使用任何现成引擎，而是用C++与OpenGL亲手构建了包括渲染器、谜题编辑器、平台层在内的整套工具链，并实现了着色器热重载以加速迭代，通过自定义基础库替换标准库显著缩短编译时间，最终在macOS与Windows上完成发布。游戏本身以学习外星逻辑为核心玩法，强调通过探索与推理掌握新规则，适合热爱底层技术、追求原理本质的开发者以及喜欢深度逻辑解谜的玩家。

PIP reviews the programmer. [](/littlestjames82sys/pippip/blob/main/examples/demo.gif) [](/littlestjames82sys/pippip/blob/main/examples/samplereportcard.svg) No AI, no models, no uploads: PIP is one Python file of plain arithmetic that reads your local git history and issues a formal managerstyle performance review of the person who wrote it. Grades, evidence, awards, and a 30day improvement plan. It is a novelty that takes its evidence seriously, and it is not for employment decisions: it grades a commit record, not a person, and it reads best when the reader is the author. Every developer keeps a work diary without knowing it: their git history. Every change is in there, with a timestamp and a little note that was supposed to explain it. PIP reads that record, locally, on your own machine, and issues a formal managerstyle performance review. With evidence. pip install onapip (or keep it isolated: pipx install onapip. The project site lives at <https://littlestjames82sys.github.io/pippip/) Then, inside any git repository: onapip Or see how a famous project's record grades out, straight from the internet: onapip psf/requests GitHub shorthand onapip https://github.com/psf/requests any git URL onapip psf/requests leaderboard rank the whole team PIP clones the repo into a temp folder, reviews it, and deletes the clone when it is done (keep keeps it, shallow 500 fetches only recent history on huge repos). Reviewing a famous project is an education: the creator of Requests grades out at a D with a Night Owl award, and his record splits into two leaderboard rows because he committed under two email addresses and the project has no mailmap to merge them. PIP counts identities the way git does. The record is the record. PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENT PLAN Dev Example pipsample 8 commits reviewed 20251014 to 20261108 Communication F 32.5 Reliability C 64.4 Followthrough B 84.3 Judgment B 83.8 Consistency D 43.0 OVERALL C 61.6 Meets some expectations. items.descZh: PIP 是一款极具创意的本地化工具，它通过读取程序员的本地 Git 提交历史，为其生成一份正式的、类似经理风格的绩效改进计划（PIP）。核心功能完全基于本地确定性的纯算术分析，无需 AI 支持，也无需任何网络上传，绝对保护代码隐私。它能从沟通、可靠性、执行力、判断力与一致性等维度生成详细的成绩单与 30 天改进计划，如示例样本般给出沟通 F（32.5分）和综合 C（61.6分）的直观量化评分。此外，它支持快速克隆并分析 GitHub 上的知名项目，还能为团队生成提交记录排行榜。这非常适合开发者用于个人提交习惯的自我反思、团队趣味评优，以及对隐私要求极高的离线代码行为分析。
items.quote: 每种工具审查你的代码。PIP 审查的是程序员。
